title: Passwords that hold + 2FA that helps
body:
THE IDEA: One strong, unique password per site, stored in a password manager, plus a second factor (2FA) on everything that matters. The manager solves reuse; 2FA solves theft — even if someone steals your password, they still lack the second proof. Start with email, because every password reset flows through it.

IN PRACTICE: Not all second factors are equal. SMS codes travel through your phone carrier, so an attacker who cons the carrier (a SIM-swap) receives your codes. An authenticator app keeps codes on your device, and a hardware key keeps them on a key you touch. Order of strength: key, then app, then SMS, then nothing. Tonight: install one manager, move email to app-based 2FA, and write the backup codes on paper — paper survives dead phones and can't be phished.

WATCH OUT: Screenshots of backup codes in your camera roll or chat are just passwords with extra steps. Anyone who reads your photos owns the accounts. Paper in a drawer beats cloud notes for these codes.

quiz.q: Your email offers SMS codes or an authenticator app. Which holds up better against SIM-swap theft?
What does the CIA triad's 'Confidentiality' mean here?
choices: Only the right people can read it

title: Spot phishing without clicking
body:
THE IDEA: Phishing doesn't break computers, it borrows your trust. Every phish has the same skeleton: a sender that looks almost right, a link or file that does the work, and urgency that stops you checking. Learn the skeleton and you spot the species.

IN PRACTICE: Read the sender letter by letter — attackers swap lookalikes, like a capital I for a lowercase L (myschooI vs myschool). Never tap the link; hover it on desktop or long-press on mobile to preview where it really goes. Treat urgency plus an attachment as a full stop: lock warnings, grade scares, prize claims. The safe move is always the same — ignore the message, open the official site yourself, and check there.

WATCH OUT: Real schools, banks, and game studios never ask for passwords or one-time codes over chat, call, or email reply. Anyone who does is either the attacker or failing their own training.

quiz.q: A message says 'account locked, verify now' with a short link. Safest move?
choices: Type the official site address yourself
Reply with your ID to confirm

title: CIA triad, malware names, encryption in plain words
body:
THE IDEA: The CIA triad is three promises. Confidentiality: only the right people can read it. Integrity: nobody secretly changed it. Availability: it's there when you need it. Every attack breaks at least one leg, and naming the leg tells you what to fix.

IN PRACTICE: Ransomware scrambles your files and sells the key back — that's availability burning. A trojan pretends to be homework (grades.xlsx.exe) while installing a backdoor — that's confidentiality and integrity both. Worms crawl networks alone; viruses need you to run a host file. Encryption scrambles readable text with a key (reversible with the key); hashing makes a one-way fingerprint (same input, same fingerprint, no way back) — which is why logins store hashes, not passwords.

WATCH OUT: Don't mix the tools up. Encryption protects reading, hashing proves identity and integrity, and backups protect availability. Each quiz wrong answer here is a real mix-up beginners make.

quiz.q: Ransomware primarily breaks which leg of the triad?
Hashing a password is best described as?

title: Recruit checkpoint
body:
THE IDEA: This gate proves the habits stuck: refusing code-beggars, unique passwords with 2FA, naming malware by behavior, and knowing what a key unlocks. Pass at 70% and the terminal band opens — fail and the same four ideas are waiting one screen back, no penalty.

IN PRACTICE: Read each scenario as a person, not a rule. Who is asking, through what channel, and what happens if you say nothing for an hour? 'Nothing bad' is the signature of a phish's fake urgency. There is no terminal in this band by design — shells start at level 11.

quiz.q: Someone calls claiming to be IT and asks for your one-time code. You?
choices: Read it out, they sound senior
Refuse and report via official channel
Ask them to text from personal number
Save passwords in browser on shared PC

title: OSI and TCP/IP without tears
body:
THE IDEA: Networks stack jobs in layers so each layer can be reasoned about alone. OSI names seven; TCP/IP runs four. For this whole platform you need the working map: Link moves frames to neighbors, Internet (IP) routes packets across networks, Transport (TCP for ordered, UDP for fire-and-forget) handles delivery style, Application (HTTP, DNS, SSH) holds the actual conversations.

IN PRACTICE: When a lab prints '80/tcp open', read it layer by layer: IP answered (Internet), the TCP handshake completed (Transport), something speaks HTTP (Application). Port numbers live at Transport; service names live at Application. That single sentence is the whole skill behind every scan readout you will meet here.

WATCH OUT: UDP has no handshake and no retries — DNS and game traffic love it for speed. If a question mentions ordering or reliability, the answer is wearing TCP clothes.

quiz.q: TCP vs UDP in one line?
choices: TCP orders and retries, UDP fires and forgets

quiz.q: An IP address lives at which layer?

title: Linux: ls, cd, cat without fear
body:
THE IDEA: A Linux shell is a conversation: you type a verb, it answers in text. Five verbs carry this band: pwd (where am I), ls (what's here), ls -la (including the hidden dotfiles), cd (move), cat (print a file). Flags look like flag{...} and hide where beginners don't look.

IN PRACTICE: Open the linux-basics lab and run the loop yourself: pwd, then ls, then ls -la — spot .note, the dotfile plain ls hid. cat readme.txt points at /home/recruit/flag.txt; cat that path and submit what you find in the flag box. Every command here runs against a fake machine we ship — the same keystrokes on a real network you don't own would be someone else's incident.

WATCH OUT: Paths matter. readme.txt and /home/recruit/flag.txt are different files in different rooms. Tab-completion and pwd keep you oriented; guessing keeps you lost.

quiz.q: Which command lists files including hidden ones?
Which command prints a text file?

title: Ports and protocols you will actually meet
body:
THE IDEA: An IP address finds the machine; a port finds the program. Memorize the doors you will actually meet: 22 SSH (remote shells), 53 DNS (names to numbers), 80 HTTP and 443 HTTPS (the web, plain and encrypted), 3306 MySQL (databases). Pair each with its layer from the OSI lesson: numbers are Transport, names are Application.

IN PRACTICE: The scan-sim lab knocks on a fictional target and prints a table — your job is reading, not knocking. 80/tcp open means a web server may answer; 22/tcp closed means SSH won't. The next move after an open web port is always the same here: probe the practice web app we ship, never a real host.

WATCH OUT: HTTPS is 443, not 80 and not 8080. DNS is 53. Quiz options love swapping these three.

title: Permissions and tiny scripts
body:
THE IDEA: Every Linux file wears a permission string: rwx (read, write, execute) repeated for user, group, and other. chmod +x adds execute. And a script is just commands saved in a file — a three-line bash loop beats clicking fifty times, and five lines of Python beat bash for text.

IN PRACTICE: Read -rw------- as a sentence: owner reads and writes, group and others get nothing — the only safe shape for a private key. Read -rwxrwxrwx as an alarm: everyone can execute it, so if root ever runs it, anyone's edit becomes root's action. That alarm is exactly the privesc-sim lab waiting in Specialist.

WATCH OUT: +x grants execution, it doesn't run anything by itself. And scripting pays off for repetition of safe local checks — never for guessing someone else's credentials.

choices: Repeating a safe check many times

title: Operator checkpoint + terminal gate
body:
THE IDEA: This gate checks the hands, not just the head: default ports, orientation commands, and reading one permission string cold. Pass at 70% plus the linux-basics flag and Analyst opens — where hints start costing real coins and the training wheels loosen.

IN PRACTICE: If -rw------- versus -rwxrwxrwx doesn't parse instantly yet, walk one more lap through the permissions lesson before attempting. Speed here is fluency, and fluency is the whole Operator game.

title: OSINT without stalking
body:
THE IDEA: OSINT is collection from public sources with receipts: every fact gets a source plus a date, guesses are labeled guesses, and the line stops before contact, trickery, or intrusion. Footprinting a target means mapping what it exposes — site maps, staff pages, DNS-style records — before deciding anything.

IN PRACTICE: Work fictional Alon Freight in the lab the way a professional writes it up: public sitemap first, then subdomains of the practice target, then a notes file with one line per fact. Messaging an employee to extract answers is social engineering, not research — it fails this lesson on purpose.

WATCH OUT: Real people and real companies are off limits everywhere on this site. The discipline of stopping is the skill being graded.

choices: Messaging an employee to trick them
Listing public subdomains of the practice target

title: Enumeration and reading scan output
body:
THE IDEA: Enumeration turns one address into an inventory: hostnames, open ports, services, versions. It sits between recon and probing — you list before you touch. Reading a scan table is the analyst's daily bread: port, state, service, then what that service suggests.

IN PRACTICE: The scan-sim lab prints an nmap-style table for fictional 10.13.0.5: 22 closed, 80 open, 443 closed. Translation: SSH is out, a web server is in — so the next step is probe --web against our practice app, then the vuln notes. Hint prices here run 1.5x Operator because the reads are longer.

WATCH OUT: Enumeration answers 'what is there', never 'break in'. The correct next step after an open port is always more reading — on our targets only.

quiz.q: Next step after finding 80/tcp open on the practice box?
choices: Probe the web app we ship
Try default passwords on real routers

title: SQL injection and XSS, safely demoed
body:
THE IDEA: Two web bugs, one shared root cause: trusting user input. SQL injection happens when a login builds its query by gluing strings — a crafted input rewrites the question the database hears. Cross-site scripting happens when a page echoes input as raw HTML — a crafted comment becomes code in someone else's browser.

IN PRACTICE: In our practice app, typing ' OR '1'='1 into the demo login reshapes the query (string-built, no parameters — that's the bug). Dropping <script> into the demo comment box and watching it execute on reload is stored XSS in miniature. The fixes sit beside each bug: parameterized queries for SQLi, output escaping plus Content-Security-Policy for XSS. Never test these keystrokes on real sites — the lab resets with a button, the real world doesn't.

WATCH OUT: Hiding the login page fixes nothing; the glued string is still there. Fixes live in code, not in obscurity.

choices: Saved then shown to others without escaping

title: CSRF and the practice app
body:
THE IDEA: Cross-Site Request Forgery rides your own logged-in session. You visit an attacker's page; it silently fires a request at a site where you're authenticated — change email, transfer, delete — wearing your cookies. The defense proves intent: anti-CSRF tokens plus SameSite cookies, with sensitive actions re-checked server-side.

IN PRACTICE: The practice app demos a forged 'change email' request succeeding without a token, then failing with one. Notice the chain this lesson demands: request plus session plus defense, all three at once — roughly double the Operator depth. SameSite=Lax (which this very site uses) is part of the same answer.

WATCH OUT: CSRF needs no password theft and no XSS. 'But they never logged in as me' is exactly why it works — the browser volunteers your session.

choices: Your live session on another site

title: Analyst checkpoint
body:
THE IDEA: The gate to Specialist checks reading plus fixing: what an open port implies, what kills SQLi, what kills reflected XSS. Pass at 70% with the scan-sim flag in hand. Past this point, recall stops being enough — Specialist grades multi-step chains.

IN PRACTICE: If any fix answer feels like magic words, reread its lesson's fix paragraph once. Analyst rewards mechanism over vocabulary.

quiz.q: Simulated scan shows 80/tcp open. That usually means?
choices: A web server may be there

title: Privilege escalation, concept-first
body:
THE IDEA: A foothold is step one; misconfigurations decide step two. Privilege escalation is mostly reading, not exploiting: stray sudo rules, world-writable scripts a higher user runs, weak service permissions, forgotten cron jobs. Check configuration before cleverness, every time.

IN PRACTICE: The privesc-sim lab hands a fake sudo -l readout and three files. id says who you are; sudo -l says what's allowed; ls -la shows a world-writable script that root's cron runs. The intended path is the boring one: the writable script. No kernel exploits, no real systems — the habit of enumerating config is the entire grade.

WATCH OUT: Random kernel exploits are how beginners brick boxes and lose shells. Enumeration first, intended path second, exotic last.

quiz.q: First privesc check on a Linux box?

title: Hashes, salts, and wordlists
body:
THE IDEA: Hashes are one-way fingerprints; salts make identical passwords hash differently and kill rainbow tables; slow algorithms (bcrypt, argon2) make each guess expensive. Fast hashes (MD5, SHA) verify files brilliantly and store passwords terribly.

IN PRACTICE: The hash-drill lab gives a known MD5 and a four-word list — crack --wordlist tries each until 'hello' matches. Then the lesson asks the grown-up question: why does this exact trick die against salted bcrypt? Because each guess costs real time and the salt voids every precomputed table. Mechanism plus the death of the easy path — double the Analyst depth.

WATCH OUT: Base64 is encoding, not hashing — it reverses instantly. MD5 is a fingerprint, not encryption — nothing to 'decrypt'.

title: Stack overflows, safely caged
body:
THE IDEA: A stack buffer overflow in one sentence: a fixed-size shelf plus unchecked input, so extra bytes spill onto the return address and the program wakes up somewhere the input chose. Real exploitation chains that with bypasses; this lesson teaches the shape plus why the shape usually fails today.

IN PRACTICE: The bof-sim lab runs a fake vulnerable program. Feed it growing inputs with run --safe until it reports control at offset 64 — no shellcode, just the offset. Then read guard.txt: canaries, ASLR, and NX each break a link of the real chain. Concept plus mitigation, nothing weaponized, nothing real.

WATCH OUT: Offset-finding is diagnostics, not payloads. Anyone selling you 'one input owns everything' is skipping the three mitigations.

choices: Adjacent stack data, possibly the return address

title: Active Directory paths, mapped not run
body:
THE IDEA: Active Directory attacks are graph problems, not password problems: users point to groups, groups to privileges, privileges to Domain Admin. Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, and token theft are just named edges on that graph. Defense is graph surgery: strong service passwords, pre-auth everywhere, tiered admins.

IN PRACTICE: Our lesson is map-reading on a drawn fictional domain. Trace the shortest path to Domain Admin, name each edge, then write the fix that deletes the most paths at once (hint: the service account with a dictionary password). You never touch a real domain here — reading maps is the transferable skill.

WATCH OUT: More tools don't beat a better map. Enumerate the graph before reaching for any edge.

quiz.q: AD attack paths are best seen as?

title: Wireless basics, hands off neighbors
body:
THE IDEA: Wireless security is handshake discipline plus skepticism of open air. WPA2/WPA3 negotiate keys; evil twins copy trusted names; open cafe Wi-Fi broadcasts your traffic to the room. Defense is boring and total: WPA3 where offered, strong pre-shared keys, VPN on open nets, forget hostile networks after.

IN PRACTICE: Read the sanitized handshake diagram in the lesson: who proves what to whom, and where an evil twin slots in. Then answer the only scenario that matters — you're on open cafe Wi-Fi and need to check something sensitive. VPN plus HTTPS, file sharing off, forget the network after. No capturing, no deauthing, no neighbor networks — ever, anywhere on this site.

WATCH OUT: 'Free WiFi' with full bars is the oldest twin in the book. Bars measure signal, not honesty.

choices: VPN + HTTPS, forget the net after
A fake AP copying a legit name

title: Specialist checkpoint
body:
THE IDEA: The gate to Red Team checks the Specialist reflexes: enumerate config before exploits, salts plus slow hashes, and AD fixes that delete whole path families. Pass at 70% with hash-drill and privesc-sim flags as proof of practice. Past this wall, PBQ-style recall can't carry you — campaigns start.

IN PRACTICE: Miss a question and don't just memorize its answer — re-run its lab command once. Specialists debug; tourists collect.

quiz.q: AD fix that kills many paths?

title: Chained attacks, MITRE-style
body:
THE IDEA: Real intrusions are campaigns, not exploits: recon, initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, defense evasion, collection, exfiltration. MITRE ATT&CK names each tactic so defenders can plant a detection at every hop — one missed hop still catches the chain.

IN PRACTICE: Take the four-step worksheet and map every lab you've cleared onto tactics: scan-sim was recon, the glued login was initial access, the cron script was persistence plus escalation. Then plan a fictional four-stage chain and, for each hop, write its detection. Double the Specialist depth: single boxes become campaigns with tripwires.

WATCH OUT: Skipping straight to exfiltration stories misses the point. Chains are graded hop by hop, and so are you.

choices: Recon, access, execution, persistence, collection, exfil
One missed hop still catches the chain

title: SSRF and deserialization, caged
body:
THE IDEA: Server-Side Request Forgery tricks a server into fetching an attacker-chosen URL — including internal ones the internet can't see. Unsafe deserialization turns crafted data into code at parse time. Both are input-trust bugs wearing server clothes, and both die to strictness: allowlists, no internal fetches, trusted schemas, signed data, never eval.

IN PRACTICE: The ssrf-sim lab ships a fake fetcher whose allowlist is off by one character. Compare what it claims to allow against what fetch --internal actually retrieves — a metadata-style file leaks a job role, and that's the flag. Then write the fix: strict allowlist plus no internal fetches, signed serializers. Fictional fetcher only; the pattern is what transfers.

WATCH OUT: Blocklists ('not localhost') lose to parser quirks every time. Allowlists win by default-deny.

choices: Trusted schemas, signed data, no eval

title: Malware analysis without malware
body:
THE IDEA: Malware analysis has a safe order: hashes and strings first (static, no execution), sandbox second (instrumented, disposable, offline), bare metal never. You're hunting persistence tricks and call-home signs, and you hash everything before uploading anywhere so samples stay trackable.

IN PRACTICE: This lesson ships printed fake reports, not samples — nothing executes, nothing can escape. List the persistence mechanism, the beaconing interval that smells like command-and-control, and why the analyst hashed before uploading. Odd beacons to newborn domains beat every other clue on the page.

WATCH OUT: Double-clicking first, disabling AV to 'see what happens', and uploading from a work machine are how case studies become incidents. Static, sandbox, never metal.

choices: Hashes/strings first, sandbox second, bare metal never

title: Cloud misconfigs vs fake AWS
body:
THE IDEA: Cloud breaches are rarely break-ins; they're open doors. World-readable storage, security groups waving everyone through, keys pasted into code and chat. The fix is least privilege plus safe defaults: block-public on, short-lived rotated keys, policies that say no unless told yes.

IN PRACTICE: The cloud-sim lab lists three fake buckets — list-buckets, then show-policy on each. One policy grants the world GetObject; quote that line, submit the flag, then write the fix: block-public defaults, tightened policy, rotated key. Fake cloud only; real account IDs never appear here.

WATCH OUT: 'Nobody knows the URL' is not access control. Obscurity has never survived a scanner.

title: Red Team checkpoint
body:
THE IDEA: The gate to Apex checks server-side thinking: SSRF fixes, cloud least-privilege, and detection-per-hop chain sense. Pass at 70% with ssrf-sim and cloud-sim flags as hands-on proof. Apex mixes everything you've done with defense under a timer.

IN PRACTICE: State each fix as a default, not a patch: allowlist by default, private by default, detections at every hop by default. Defaults survive tired engineers; patches don't.

title: Blue team: logs and incident response
body:
THE IDEA: Blue team is reading under pressure. Triage runs PICERL: prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons-learned — and order matters, because wiping before containing destroys the evidence and keeps the door. The strongest signals cluster: impossible-hour logins, fresh persistence, outbound spikes.

IN PRACTICE: The logs-sim bundle is one incident in a trench coat. grep FAIL for the pre-dawn failures, tail for the 02:14 success, timeline.txt for the cron persistence plus egress spike. Verdict: contain (isolate) first, then cure — and the one-paragraph incident note you write is the actual deliverable. Timed in the boss mission; calm reading beats fast clicking.

WATCH OUT: A single failed login is noise; fourteen plus an odd-hour success plus new persistence is a story. Triage clusters, never singles.

quiz.q: First IR move on suspected compromise?

title: Boss battle: everything chained
body:
THE IDEA: The capstone chains every band in one timed run: a hygiene call, a Linux find, a scan read, a web bug, a hash crack, a cloud policy, a log triage — seven flags, one clock, tier-1 hints only. Breadth first, hardest flag last, notes always. This is the exam the earlier checkpoints were rehearsing.

IN PRACTICE: Open with what you can clear in two minutes each and bank the momentum; park the monster flag for the middle third; spend the last stretch on triage with fresh eyes. Pass here and Prestige unlocks: back to level 1 with a permanent badge and the monthly rotator pool, so myths never idle.

WATCH OUT: Hint-first on everything is how boss runs die poor. Hints are tier-1 only — your notes are the real hint ladder.

choices: Breadth first, hardest flag last, notes always
Reset to 1 with badge + harder monthly pool

title: Apex checkpoint
body:
THE IDEA: The final gate checks the complete operator: contain before eradicate, chained offense with calm defense under time, and knowing what comes after Apex. Pass at 70% with the SOC and boss work as proof. The Prestige button on your profile is the diploma that deletes itself.

IN PRACTICE: Say each answer as an order of operations, not a slogan. Isolate, then remove cause, then recover, then write the lesson. Order is the credential.

choices: Chained offense + calm defense under time

title: Monthly rotator (prestige pool)
body:
THE IDEA: Prestige trades the crown for a harder mountain: reset to level 1 with a permanent badge, plus a monthly set with re-rolled flags, tighter timers, and tier-1 hints only. Same fictional boxes, meaner configs — the loop top players asked for.

IN PRACTICE: January's set ships in this prototype so the loop is visible: re-clear familiar boxes against new flags, post a season score, hold the myth seat. New prompts land the first of each month. Real targets remain out of scope at every prestige, forever.

choices: New flags, tighter time, minimal hints
